title: Toxicology
description: Principles of toxicology, dose–response and toxicity testing, management of poisoning, common poisons in Nigeria, and environmental and occupational toxicology.

topics.title: Principles of Toxicology
topics.summary: Dose makes the poison, dose–response, LD50, therapeutic index and toxicokinetics.

notes.b: Toxicology studies the adverse effects of chemicals on living organisms. Paracelsus stated that 'the dose makes the poison' — any substance can be toxic at sufficient dose. Toxicity may be acute (single exposure), subacute, subchronic or chronic (repeated exposure over months to years). The dose–response relationship underlies risk assessment: LD50 is the dose lethal to 50% of test animals; ED50 the dose effective in 50%; the therapeutic index (LD50/ED50 or TD50/ED50) measures safety margin. NOAEL (no-observed-adverse-effect level) is used to set acceptable daily intakes with safety (uncertainty) factors. Threshold effects contrast with non-threshold effects such as genotoxic carcinogens.
k: Paracelsus: the dose makes the poison

notes.b: Toxicokinetics describes absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion of toxicants; in overdose, processes may become saturated (zero-order kinetics). Bioactivation converts some chemicals to more toxic metabolites (paracetamol → NAPQI; methanol → formic acid; ethylene glycol → oxalic acid; organophosphorothioates such as parathion → paraoxon). Mechanisms of toxicity include enzyme inhibition (organophosphates on acetylcholinesterase, cyanide on cytochrome oxidase), receptor interaction, free-radical injury, covalent binding to macromolecules, and interference with oxygen transport (carbon monoxide, nitrite-induced methaemoglobinaemia). Target organs include liver (hepatotoxins), kidney (nephrotoxins — aminoglycosides, heavy metals), nervous system and bone marrow.

It is a measure of acute lethality.

topics.title: General Management of Poisoning
topics.summary: Resuscitation, decontamination, enhanced elimination, antidotes and toxidromes.

notes.b: Management of the poisoned patient: (1) resuscitation — ABCDE, with attention to airway protection, breathing, circulation, glucose ('don't ever forget glucose') and seizures; (2) history (substance, amount, time, route, intent — from patient, relatives, containers) and examination for toxidromes; (3) investigations (glucose, electrolytes, gases, paracetamol and salicylate levels, ECG); (4) decontamination — activated charcoal (1 g/kg) within about 1 hour for adsorbable toxins in a patient with a protected airway (not effective for iron, lithium, alcohols, acids, alkalis, hydrocarbons); gastric lavage is rarely indicated; induced vomiting (ipecac, salt water) is not recommended; whole bowel irrigation for iron or packets; skin and eye decontamination with water; (5) enhanced elimination — urinary alkalinisation (salicylates), multiple-dose activated charcoal, haemodialysis (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates); (6) specific antidotes; (7) supportive care and psychiatric assessment after self-harm. Poison information centres give advice.

Toxidromes: cholinergic (organophosphates — salivation, lacrimation, miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, fasciculations), anticholinergic (atropine, antihistamines, tricyclics — hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, tachycardia, urinary retention, delirium), opioid (miosis, respiratory depression, coma), sympathomimetic (cocaine, amphetamines — tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, mydriasis, sweating) and sedative-hypnotic. Antidotes: N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol), naloxone (opioids), flumazenil (benzodiazepines — caution with seizures), atropine and pralidoxime (organophosphates), fomepizole or ethanol (methanol, ethylene glycol), hydroxocobalamin (cyanide), methylene blue (methaemoglobinaemia), desferrioxamine (iron), digoxin-specific antibody fragments (digoxin), vitamin K (warfarin), protamine (heparin), sodium bicarbonate (tricyclics — QRS widening), oxygen (carbon monoxide), antivenom (snakebite).

Stabilising airway, breathing and circulation comes first.

topics.title: Common Poisonings in Nigeria
topics.summary: Organophosphates and paraquat, kerosene, snakebite, drug overdoses and herbal toxicity.

notes.b: Organophosphate and carbamate insecticides (e.g. 'Sniper' — dichlorvos) are commonly used in suicide attempts and accidental poisoning in Nigeria; management includes decontamination, airway support, atropine titrated to drying of chest secretions (clear chest, heart rate > 80, SBP > 80 mmHg), and early pralidoxime for organophosphates. Paraquat (herbicide) causes corrosive oral injury and progressive, often fatal lung fibrosis — avoid high-concentration oxygen. Kerosene (paraffin) ingestion is common in children because it is stored in drink bottles; the main danger is aspiration pneumonitis — never induce vomiting. Caustic ingestion (bleach, acids, alkalis) causes oesophageal burns; do not induce vomiting or neutralise. Carbon monoxide poisoning from generators in closed rooms is frequent. Contaminated or adulterated products have caused mass poisonings (e.g. diethylene glycol in paracetamol teething mixture 'My Pikin' in 2008).
k: Paraquat: lung fibrosis; avoid high O2
Kerosene: aspiration risk — don't induce vomiting

notes.b: Snakebite is a major neglected tropical disease in northern Nigeria (e.g. Gombe, Plateau, Bauchi). The carpet viper (Echis ocellatus) causes local swelling and coagulopathy — the 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) detects incoagulable blood; treatment is specific antivenom (e.g. EchiTAb), with close monitoring for anaphylaxis (adrenaline ready). Cobras (neurotoxic — ptosis, respiratory paralysis) and puff adders (tissue necrosis) also occur. Avoid tourniquets, incisions and suction. Drug overdoses: paracetamol, antimalarials (chloroquine — cardiotoxicity), tramadol (seizures, serotonin syndrome, respiratory depression), and codeine syrup misuse. Herbal remedies can cause hepatotoxicity, renal failure (e.g. aristolochic acid) or contain heavy metals; ask about them in unexplained organ failure.

topics.title: Heavy Metals and Environmental Toxicology
topics.summary: Lead, mercury, arsenic and cadmium; air and water pollutants; and chelation therapy.

notes.b: Lead: sources include artisanal gold mining (Zamfara 2010 outbreak), lead-based paint, batteries recycling, contaminated cosmetics (e.g. some eye cosmetics — 'tiro'/kohl) and water pipes; effects include anaemia (basophilic stippling, inhibition of ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase), neurotoxicity (encephalopathy, reduced IQ in children, wrist/foot drop in adults), abdominal colic and a blue gum line; treated with chelation (succimer/DMSA, calcium disodium EDTA, dimercaprol). Mercury: elemental vapour (tremor, gingivitis, erethism), methylmercury in fish (neurotoxic — Minamata disease), inorganic salts (renal damage); skin-lightening creams may contain mercury. Arsenic: contaminated groundwater (skin hyperpigmentation, keratoses, cancers), acute poisoning (vomiting, 'rice-water' diarrhoea, garlic odour, Mees' lines on nails). Cadmium: renal tubular damage, osteomalacia ('itai-itai' disease).
k: Lead: stippling, neuropathy, reduced IQ; chelation

notes.b: Air pollutants (PM2.5, ozone, NO2, SO2, carbon monoxide) cause respiratory and cardiovascular disease; household solid-fuel smoke and generator exhaust are major exposures in Nigeria. Oil spills and gas flaring in the Niger Delta contaminate water, soil and air with hydrocarbons (benzene — leukaemia; polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — cancers). Persistent organic pollutants (DDT, dioxins, PCBs) bioaccumulate and biomagnify in food chains. Aflatoxins contaminate poorly stored grains and groundnuts, causing liver cancer (especially with hepatitis B). Food adulterants of concern include calcium carbide for ripening fruit and formalin on fish. Risk assessment integrates hazard identification, dose–response, exposure assessment and risk characterisation.

topics.title: Drugs of Abuse and Toxicity Testing
topics.summary: Commonly abused substances in Nigeria, their toxicity, and regulatory toxicity testing of new chemicals.

notes.b: Commonly misused substances in Nigeria include cannabis (the most widely used illicit drug), tramadol, codeine-containing cough syrups, benzodiazepines, methamphetamine ('mkpuru mmiri'), cocaine, heroin, inhalants (glue, petrol) and alcohol; the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) enforces drug laws and NAFDAC regulates controlled medicines. Toxic effects: cannabis — psychosis in susceptible users, cannabinoid hyperemesis; stimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine) — hypertension, arrhythmias, stroke, hyperthermia, psychosis; opioids — respiratory depression; alcohol — acute intoxication, hypoglycaemia, withdrawal (tremor, seizures, delirium tremens — treat with benzodiazepines and thiamine to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy). Dependence involves tolerance, withdrawal and compulsive use despite harm.

Before approval, new drugs and chemicals undergo toxicity testing: acute toxicity (single dose, LD50 or fixed-dose/up-and-down procedures that use fewer animals), repeated-dose subacute and chronic toxicity, genotoxicity (Ames test in Salmonella for mutagenicity, micronucleus test), carcinogenicity (long-term rodent studies), reproductive and developmental toxicity (teratogenicity — the thalidomide disaster led to stricter testing), and safety pharmacology (cardiac QT effects). The 3Rs principle guides ethical animal use: Replacement, Reduction and Refinement. OECD guidelines and Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) ensure data quality; regulatory agencies such as NAFDAC review the data.
